hints.text: Start with typography. Set the headline before you choose a single colour.
Try a 60 / 30 / 10 colour distribution: dominant, supporting, accent.
Sketch three thumbnail concepts at postage-stamp size. If it does not work small, it will not work large.
Make a monochrome version first. If the hierarchy fails in grey, colour will not rescue it.
Design the simplest possible version, then decide what genuinely needs adding.
Double your white space. Then look again before reducing it.
Pick one element to be the hero and deliberately shrink everything else.
Increase the size difference between your largest and smallest type. Timid hierarchy reads as indecision.
Align everything to a grid, then break it exactly once, on purpose.
Read the brief again and highlight the single most important sentence. Design that.
Look at the piece at 10% zoom. What still reads is your real hierarchy.
Flip the canvas horizontally. Balance problems become obvious immediately.
Remove the image and see whether the layout still communicates.
Take the boldest idea you rejected in the first ten minutes and give it twenty more.
Constrain yourself to two type sizes for the next fifteen minutes.
Use one accent colour on exactly one element — the thing you most want clicked or read.
Set the copy first with placeholder styling. Real content changes every layout decision.
Look at three references from outside the client's industry, not inside it.
Ask what the piece would look like if the client had half the budget and twice the confidence.
Give the composition one clear diagonal or one clear axis. Choose, do not hedge.
Zoom out and squint. The blurred shapes should still show a reading order.
Try setting the headline in the body typeface at a large size before reaching for a display face.
Write the one-sentence rationale now. If you cannot, the concept is not resolved yet.
Cut the number of elements by a third and see what you actually miss.
Check the smallest deliverable first — it usually dictates the whole system.
Place the least interesting element last. Backgrounds are decisions, not defaults.

solution_hints: A strong answer usually leads with one idea, not three competing ones.
Most successful versions of this brief solve the hierarchy before the styling.
The restrictions are the interesting part of this brief — lean into them rather than working around them.
Consider what the piece looks like next to the client's competitors, not on a clean presentation board.
If two deliverables look unrelated, the system is not finished.
